lines: The wind came in <wavy>hard enough</wavy> to make the whole village taste like dust.
No rain here, just grit in the shutters and everyone checking their eyes.
The sand got everywhere, but people found their way indoors.
Harsh wind can scare a village nearly as well as thunder. We are still here.
We are sweeping doorways and counting heads after that wall of dust.
The storm turned every path into a guess for a while.
People are still shaking sand from their clothes and worry from their voices.
The wind has passed, but the dust is taking its time leaving.
A sandstorm makes even familiar doors feel far away.
We kept low, covered our faces, and waited for the village to reappear.
Dust came through gaps we did not know the houses had.
We tied cloth over our faces before crossing the square.
The wind erased every path within minutes.
Animals were brought indoors when the fences began to vanish.
Nobody opened a door without someone holding it from inside.
Sand filled the well cover and every uncovered chest.
We found roof pieces half a field away after the wind stopped.
People called between houses because we could not see each other.
Cleanup began with shovels at every doorstep.
The village still tastes of grit when the wind picks up.
The wind threw sand at the windows. I did not like the sound.
I got dust in my mouth even inside. How does it do that?
The grown-ups said cover my face, so I did.
It was like the ground tried to <wavy>fly away</wavy>.
I am okay, but my hair feels crunchy.
The outside disappeared, and I thought that was very rude.
I tried to look out, but the window only showed angry dust.
The wind sounded like it was scratching the whole house.
I stayed inside because the sand was being mean.
Next time the ground starts flying, I am hiding under a blanket.
Sand came under the door even after we stuffed cloth there.
I could not see the well from our window.
We wore scarves over our mouths inside the house.
The wind made the roof sound like it was growling.
Someone gave me a brush to sweep one corner over and over.
All my pockets had sand in them afterward.
I slept beside the wall farthest from the storm.
The square looked like a different place when we came outside.
We found one of my toys near the crops the next day.
I never knew sand could be that loud.
The snow came down hard, but the hearths held and the doors stayed shut.
Cold frightens <pulse>slowly</pulse>. We are checking fingers, roofs, and firewood.
The village went white and quiet for a while. <italic>Quiet is not always peace.</italic>
Everyone is chilled, but accounted for. Warmth matters now.
We are clearing paths before the snow hides what people need.
The storm made every roof carry more than it should.
People are sharing firewood and pretending they are not worried about the next gust.
Snow softens sound, but it does not soften danger.
The paths are buried, so we are making new ones one shovel at a time.
We made it through the worst of it. Now comes the cold work after.
Snow buried the lower windows before morning.
We marked doors with lanterns so nobody lost the path between houses.
Several roofs needed clearing before the weight became dangerous.
The animals crowded together while we carried in extra feed.
People shared hearths when the cold reached the smaller homes.
No one traveled alone while the snow hid the village edges.
The bell rope froze stiff before anyone needed it.
We dug paths to the well and the healer first.
Work stopped until every household had enough fuel.
When the sky cleared, the village was white and exhausted.
